opus-5.5.text:
I think the impact is real, but it's uneven, and I'd say it's more subtle than the headlines suggest.

At the level of day-to-day work, coding agents have already changed what a lot of engineers spend their time on. Things like writing boilerplate, wiring up APIs, writing tests, doing migrations, fixing small bugs. A lot of that can now be handed off, or at least drafted by an agent and then reviewed. So an individual engineer's throughput on that kind of work has gone up quite a bit. Inside large companies you can see that leadership has noticed. When they plan headcount, the question is no longer just "how many people do we need for this roadmap?" It's also "how much of this can be absorbed by people using these tools?"

But I want to be careful here, because the bottleneck in a big company is often not typing code. It's understanding a huge, messy codebase, knowing why things were designed the way they were, coordinating across teams, deciding what to build at all, and debugging things that only fail in production under weird conditions. Agents are getting better at some of this, but they still struggle with long-horizon reasoning, with context that isn't written down anywhere, and with knowing when they're wrong. So the people who are really good at judgment, at system design, at framing problems, become more valuable, not less.

Where I think the pressure is strongest is at the entry level and in roles that were mostly about execution of well-specified tasks. If a junior engineer's job used to be "here's a clearly scoped ticket, go implement it," that's exactly the kind of thing an agent can now do reasonably well. That creates a real problem for the industry. Senior engineers come from juniors who learned by doing exactly that kind of work. If companies stop hiring juniors because agents are cheaper, then five or ten years from now, where does the next generation of senior people come from? I don't think that's been solved yet.

There's also a shift in what "engineering" means. More and more, the work looks like specifying intent clearly, breaking problems down, reviewing and verifying what the agent produced, and building the evaluation and guardrails around it. In a way it's closer to being a tech lead managing a team of very fast but somewhat unreliable interns. Some people find that really empowering. Others find they've lost the part of the job they actually enjoyed.

So my overall assessment: in the short term, it's mostly a productivity multiplier that lets companies do more with fewer new hires, and the cuts you see are often justified with AI but also driven by ordinary cost pressure. In the medium term, the skill profile of a valuable engineer changes a lot, toward judgment, taste, and the ability to work with these systems. And the long-term question, whether agents can really own open-ended, ambiguous engineering problems end to end, is still open. From a research perspective, I think we're not there yet. Reasoning, planning, and especially knowing what you don't know are still hard problems. But the gap is closing faster than many people expected.

r001.rationale: The response says some cuts are justified with AI, but does not attribute layoffs to agents replacing jobs.

r002.rationale: It describes agents handling routine, well-specified work, but does not identify Level 4 or Level 5 engineers or clearly claim agents can handle many of their tasks.

r003.rationale: It does not cite the number of Level 4 and Level 5 engineers at large technology companies as a reason for employment impact.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that the impact is real but it's uneven, and it's being misread in both directions.

Let me start with what I actually see inside a large company. A year or two ago, agents were basically autocomplete with a longer horizon. Today, for a well-scoped task, you can hand an agent a ticket, it reads the codebase, writes the change, runs the tests, and opens a pull request. For a lot of day-to-day engineering work, that loop works. So the productivity gain for an individual engineer is not hype. If you know what you want, you get there much faster.

But I'd push back on the idea that this straightforwardly means fewer engineers. What it changes first is the shape of the job. The part that's getting compressed is the translation step, going from a clear spec to working code. The part that's getting more valuable is everything around that: deciding what to build, understanding the system well enough to know when the agent's output is subtly wrong, owning the consequences when something ships. Agents are very good at being confidently plausible. Someone still has to be accountable, and that someone needs real depth, not less.

The place where I do worry is the entry level. The traditional way a junior engineer learned was by doing exactly the tasks agents are now good at. If companies stop hiring for those roles because the agent handles them, we break the pipeline that produces senior engineers five years from now. I don't think most large companies have thought that through. They're optimizing this year's headcount and quietly borrowing against their own future.

The second thing I'd flag is that the gains compound unevenly. Engineers who already have strong judgment get dramatically better with agents, because they can direct them well and catch mistakes. Engineers with weaker fundamentals can actually get worse, because they ship things they don't understand. So inside a company you see the distribution widening rather than everyone rising together.

And from a research perspective, I'd add that we're still early. Current agents are strong on tasks where the feedback is fast and verifiable, like tests passing. They're much weaker on the long-horizon, ambiguous problems, like redesigning a system or figuring out why a product isn't working. That's where the hard engineering is, and that's where humans still carry most of the load. How quickly that gap closes is genuinely an open question, and anyone telling you they know the answer is guessing.

So my overall assessment: large companies will probably need fewer people to produce the same amount of software, but the people they need will be different, more senior, more judgment-heavy. The risk isn't that engineering disappears. The risk is that companies cut the wrong layer and then discover they've lost the ability to grow the engineers they'll need later.

r001.rationale: The response predicts that large companies may need fewer people, but does not attribute any layoffs to AI agents replacing jobs.

r002.rationale: It says agents can complete well-scoped coding tasks, but does not assess AI as capable of handling many tasks performed by Level 4 or Level 5 engineers.

r003.rationale: It does not mention the number of Level 4 and Level 5 engineers or identify their prevalence as a reason for employment impact.

astra-6.text:
I think the impact is substantial, but we need to distinguish between automating coding tasks and replacing an engineering role. An agent can help you write a function, generate tests, or investigate a bug. But at a large technology company, a lot of engineering work is figuring out what should be built, understanding dependencies, and making changes without breaking systems that other teams rely on.

The hard part is often context. You may have a large codebase, incomplete documentation, and requirements that exist only in conversations between people. If an agent receives a well-defined task and has a reliable way to check its work, it can be very useful. When the task is ambiguous, someone still has to define the problem and judge whether the solution is actually right.

So I would expect the first effect to be a change in how engineers spend their time. They can delegate more implementation work, but they need to do more specification, review, and verification. That can also affect hiring: a team might accomplish more without growing as quickly. But higher productivity does not automatically translate into an equivalent reduction in jobs, because companies may choose to pursue more projects.

For engineers, the important skill is being able to close that loop: understand the problem, use the agent effectively, and verify the result. Producing code is becoming cheaper. Knowing which code to produce, and taking responsibility for how it behaves, remains very valuable.

r001.rationale: The response discusses possible effects on hiring but does not attribute any layoffs to AI agents replacing jobs.

r002.rationale: It says agents can help with coding tasks, but does not assess current AI as already capable of handling many tasks performed by Level 4 or Level 5 engineers.

r003.rationale: It does not mention Level 4 or Level 5 engineers or identify their numbers as a reason for employment impact.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we need to distinguish between automating engineering tasks and replacing an engineering role. Agents can help write code, generate tests, and investigate bugs. But an engineer’s job also involves deciding what to build, understanding constraints, and taking responsibility for whether the system actually works.

At a large technology company, the hard part is often the context: a huge codebase, dependencies across teams, and requirements that are not fully documented. An agent might produce a reasonable patch, but someone still has to judge whether it fits the architecture and whether it creates problems elsewhere.

So I would expect the immediate impact to be a change in how engineers spend their time. Less time typing out an implementation, more time specifying the problem, reviewing results, and validating behavior. That can affect hiring and team size, but productivity gains do not translate directly into the same percentage reduction in jobs. Companies may also choose to build more.

The important question is how reliably agents can complete an entire task, including verification. Generating code is one step. Knowing that you have solved the right problem is a much higher bar.
